claims.text: An active-learning MLIP trained on ab initio liquid configurations near melting will capture the atomic arrangements of multicomponent HEA liquids better than traditional EAM potentials.
Using high-dimensional descriptors such as SOAP enables the MLIP to represent subtle many-body interactions.
The proposed MLIP will improve reference–target phase-space overlap relative to EAM references used in TOR-TILD.
Improved phase-space overlap will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD's EAM references.
The MLIP should be trained iteratively on ab initio molecular-dynamics configurations sampled from 0.9 to 1.1 times the melting temperature.
The method is applicable to equiatomic or nearly equiatomic multicomponent HEAs between approximately 0.9 and 1.1 Tm.
Near melting, multicomponent HEAs can exhibit substantial structural and chemical configurational diversity.
Nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles undergo strong structural and chemical evolution, pronounced diffusion, and surface-layer melting at high temperature.
A trained MLIP can map the many-body interactions of ab initio liquid configurations onto a potential-energy surface that closely mirrors the target ab initio phase space.
Active learning identifies and adds configurations from underrepresented regions of configurational space.
Traditional EAM potentials used by TOR-TILD inadequately represent the configurational diversity of ab initio HEA liquids.
The inadequate representation by TOR-TILD EAM references causes significant thermodynamic-integration mismatch.
The MLIP will reduce the free-energy integration mismatch to below approximately 10 meV per atom.
Successful elemental and binary liquid calculations with MLIPs provide evidence that the method should improve HEA liquid references.
The method may fail to capture rare liquid configurations or extrapolate to compositions and temperatures far outside 0.9–1.1 Tm.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing MLIP-reference free energies with full ab initio thermodynamic-integration free energies and by measuring MLIP–ab initio phase-space overlap.
Failure to achieve a mismatch below approximately 10 meV per atom or a statistically significant overlap improvement over the EAM reference would falsify the hypothesis.
